messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Specifying a location dependent tau and kappa, with a user generated function
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Specifying a location dependent tau and kappa, with a user generated function
messages.body_plain:
On Wed, Jan 31, 2018 at 5:17 PM, Finn Lindgren <finn.l...@gmail.com> wrote:
> OK, so if I interpret that correctly, you have _known_ constant
> offsets, and _no_ parameters that need estimating? Not even
> multipliers like
>   kappa(s) = exp(theta[1] - theta[3] * norm_b_grad(s))
>   tau(s) = exp(theta[2] + theta[3] * norm_b_grad(s))
> ?
>

Yes, at this point we do not need to estimate any parameters, and can assume that the offsets are known constants.

> The piecewise constantness of norm_b_grad is basically ok; you may
> want to have some odd behaviour at the discontinuities, but that's
> hard to avoid.
>
> First, project norm_b_grad onto the triangulation, to give
> norm_b_grad_on_mesh. Exactly how to do that has several possibilities.
>
> The most basic is to evaluate the function at the mesh nodes:
>   for (k in seq_len(nrow(mesh$loc)))
>     norm_b_grad_on_mesh[k] <- norm_b_grad(mesh$loc[k, ])
> Another option, that will give nicer behaviour at the continuities, is
> to approximate a projection based on integrals over the triangles.
> Let s_k and w_k be some numerical integration scheme points and
> weights, and let phi_k(s) be the triangular basis functions,
> and let z(s) be norm_b_grad(s).
>
> One could consider building the approximation from the point of view
> of the mesh, by "pulling" information at the individual points onto
> the mesh, like when evaluating z(s) at the mesh nodes, see above.
>
> For high-resolution covariates as input to kappa and tau (global
> elevation map) the most robust method I've used has been this simple
> weighting (it's not quite the full least-squares projection, but
> rather something simpler and more local) that is mare akin to
> "pushing" the information onto the mesh.
>
>   int_domain psi_k(s) z(s) ds / int_domain psi(s) ds
>   \approx
>   sum_k w_k psi_k(s_k) z(s_k) / sum_k w_k psi_k(s_k)
>
> An additional benefit of this approach is that it's much easier to
> implement; let w_k = 1, and place s_k in a dense lattice covering the
> domain, let's call them integ_loc:
>
> integ_loc <- ... ## expand.grid or inla.mesh.lattice, for example.
> integ_A <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh, loc=integ_loc) ## Computes psi_k(s_k)
> integ_z <- ... ## Evaluate norm_b_grad at the integ_loc points
> z_on_mesh <- as.vector(integ_A %*% z) / rowSums(integ_A)
>
> The parameterless model is simply given by (in the inla.spde2.matern call)
>
> B.kappa = matrix(constant_kappa - z_on_mesh, mesh$n, 1)
> B.tau = matrix(constant_tau + z_on_mesh, mesh$n, 1)
>
> This just specifies a known offset in the log-scale.
>
> With parameters (see beginning of message):
>
> B.kappa = cbind(0, 1, 0, -z_on_mesh)
> B.tau = cbind(0, 0, 1, +z_on_mesh)
>
> Hopefully this should get you going a bit?
>

Thank you for the detailed explanation of these options. This is certainly enough to get us started, and hopefully succeed.

> Finn

>
>
>
> On 31 January 2018 at 22:35, Vikram Garg <vikram...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Hello Dr. Lindgren,
> >                               I can provide a little more context about the
> > problem I am trying to solve. My objective is to generate samples from a
> > distribution with a non-stationary covariance. The specific parameter being
> > modeled is a turbulent mixing parameter that arises in ocean dynamics, and
> > hence we have a large problem size and spatially varying structure, handling
> > which requires INLA's capabilities.
> >
> > We would like to model the non-stationary covariance of the turbulent mixing
> > parameter as follows. From our ocean model, we will output the pointwise
> > norm of the bathymetry gradient ( norm_b_grad(s) ) over the region of
> > interest. The INLA parameter kappa (~local correlation length) will be set
> > as:
> >
> > kappa(s) = exp(constant - norm_b_grad(s) ),
> >
> > whereas the parameter tau (~local marginal variance) will be set as.
> >
> > tau(s) = exp(constant + norm_b_grad(s) )
> >
> > Regarding the smoothness of norm_b_grad(s), it is the norm of the gradient
> > of a C0 piecewise linear function, and hence is itself a discontinuous
> > piecewise constant function, i.e. not particularly smooth.
> >
> > Thanks.
> >
> >
> > On Wed, Jan 31, 2018 at 3:59 PM, Finn Lindgren <finn.l...@gmail.com>
> > wrote:
> >>
> >> It depends on precisely which mathematical model you want to implement.
> >>
> >> Any log-linear model is fine, where your own function is used as a
> >> “covariate”,
> >> and where it is smooth enough to be well approximated on the triangle
> >> domain.
> >> In this case this would simply feed straight into the B.tau and B.kappa
> >> matrices.
> >>
> >> If you need a more general nonlinear parameterisation, you’d need to use
> >> an rgeneric model construction that explicitly constructs the precision
> >> matrix using your own tau and kappa, and the output from inla.mesh.fem() (or
> >> some other method for constructing the precision)
> >>
> >> If you can give more details on how your user defined function depends on
> >> parameters that are to be estimated by inla, it will be easier to give more
> >> specific advice.
> >>
> >> Finn
> >>
> >> On 31 Jan 2018, at 21:52, Vikram Garg <vikram...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >>
> >> Hello,
> >>          I have been following the example in Section 2.3.2 of the SPDE
> >> tutorial (http://www.r-inla.org/examples/tutorials/spde-tutorial) which
> >> shows how R-INLA can handle a non-stationary covariance, by making the
> >> parameters tau and kappa as location dependent.
> >>
> >> In that example, tau is set to be tau_i = exp( theta_1 + theta_3 *
> >> sin(pi*x) ) where x is the spatial location (Pg 53).
> >>
> >> Here the preexisting sin(x) function in R is used to represent the
> >> non-stationarity. However, I would like to employ a user defined function,
> >> because tau in my problem depends on the output of another simulation
> >> package. I would like to try the following solution:
> >>
> >> 1) Read in the external field which specifies tau.
> >> 2) Build a function in R which evaluates this field at an arbitrary point
> >> using an interpolation approach.
> >> 3) Pass this function to the spde object in R-INLA.
> >>
> >> Would such an approach result in any issues/incompatibility ?
> >>
> >> Thanks.

messages.body_plain:
Hello

I want to fit spatio-temporal model based on following equation:
y=xB+e A+ epsilon
where dimension as follow:
y:T*N
x: T*K
B:K*N
e: T*r
A:r*N
epsilon:T*N
s.t: N:number of spatial points   T:time points   r: autoregressive coefficient (here consider r=1)
I want to use below prior for parameters:
rw1 for B.
rw1 for A.
ar1 for A.
In other words, i have two spatial prior one for B and one for A and also temporal prior(ar1) for A.
Finally, i need to map posterior mean for every column of matrix x.

I write this model using INLA: (for e.g. k=2)

formula <- y~

x1+x2+  #each column of x

f(ID.spatial,model="rw1",graph=?) + #spatial prior for B

f(ID.time1,model="ar1") +  # temporal modeling of A (AR(1))

f(ID.time2,model="iid")+  # Unstructrued noise

f(ID.time3,model="rw1",graph=?) # spatial prior for A

Finally, i need mapping posterior mean for x1 and x2 based on spatial points(in above equation N is number of spatial points).
I have two problem about this:
1) How do i define neighboring graph for spatial section? (about this, note i have just coordinates of points and i read section 6.1 from "Spatial and spatio-temporal Bayesian models with R-INLA" <https://books.google.com/books?hl=en&lr=&id=--HuBgAAQBAJ&oi=fnd&pg=PA259&dq=spatial+and+temporal+using+r+inla&ots=VTAEJ5tgQW&sig=lbFV4ftzZz1qEYq1Ok-SHnJ9KX0> but unfortunately i couldn't solve my problem)
2) How do i map posterior mean for x1 and x2?

Could any one please guide me about these?
Thank you.

messages.subject_clean: Confused trying to implement Multinomial - Logistic Normal Mixed Effects Model
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I an new to R-INLA and am having a hell of a time trying to figure out how to code a specific model.

I have data in the form of a matrix of counts Y where Y_ij represents the counts assigned to category j in sample i.
N is the total number of rows (samples).
D is the total number of categories (i.e., Y has D columns)
I also have two vectors of length N (X and Z) which are both categorical (e.g., they are vectors of integers with Q and M categories respectively).

I would like to fit the following model (just showing the likelihood):

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-Eo522WsMpfQ/Wntc414syyI/AAAAAAAAA9c/SGozP2E8C9w29U_8LZ18sC64DzpBA9MCgCLcBGAs/s1600/Y_i_%2526_sim_text_M.png>

Here Y_i refers to the i-th row of Y, π_i is a vector satisfying sum(π_i) = 1, \phi^-1 represents a softmax transform (or really a bijective softmax - where one element is set to zero for identifiability). Under this transformation (\phi) π_i is transformed to the D-1 dimensional vector η_i. β^(X_i)  and γ^(Z_i) represent D-1 dimensional vectors corresponding to the random coefficients for the factors X and Z respectively. Thus β is a Q x (D-1) matrix and γ is a M x (D-1) matrix. In addition there is added random noise in the form of ϵ which is sample specific (again ϵ_i is a D-1 dimensional vector).

Is it possible to infer this model in R-INLA? I have read through the FAQ here (http://www.r-inla.org/faq#TOC-I-have-multinomial-data-but-I-cannot-find-the-multinomial-likelihood-isn-t-it-available-) but this does not go over how to write this model for a categorical predictor (e.g., X and Z) where they end up being matricies (which in the Poisson formulation have rows that must sum to zero). I tried to get my head around the alli multinomial example but I must say I found it extremely confusing. Any help would be much appreciated.

Thank you!

Justin Silverman

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for those files.
I think I made some real progress by looking over those and taking a much closer look at the alli.R example.

Here is what I have so far:

idx2map <-  function(i,j,d){
  ## this function goes from the two index [i,j] to one index
  return (i + (j-1)*d)
}
map2idx <- function(m, d){
  ## this function goes from one index to two indicies [i,j]
  i <- (m-1)%%d+1
  j <- (m-i)/d+1
  return(cbind(i,j))

}

idx = rep(1:n, times = d)
jdx = rep(1:d, each=n)

X.inla <- rep(X[,1], times=d)
Z.inla <- rep(Z[,1], times=d)

Y.inla <- data.frame(y = c(as.matrix(Y)), idx = idx, jdx = jdx,
                     X = X.inla, Z = Z.inla)

# Create Beta Indicies
# Beta is Q x D matrix
# Gamma is an M x D matrix
# Epsilon is N x D matrix
Y.inla <- Y.inla %>%
  mutate(beta = idx2map(X, jdx, q),
         gamma = idx2map(Z, jdx, m),
         epsilon = idx2map(idx, jdx, n))

Y.inla[Y.inla[,"X"]==1,"beta"] <- NA
Y.inla[Y.inla[,"jdx"]==1,"beta"] <- NA
Y.inla[Y.inla[,"jdx"]==1,"gamma"] <- NA
Y.inla[Y.inla[,"jdx"]==1,"epsilon"] <- NA

formula = y ~ -1 +

  ## I believe the following is required to ensure equality between the multinomial
  ## formulation and the poisson formulation

  f(idx, model = "iid", hyper=list(prec = list(initial = log(0.000001), fixed=TRUE))) +
  ## Now add in the beta terms
  f(beta, constr=FALSE, hyper=list(prec = list(initial = log(0.01), fixed=TRUE))) +
  f(gamma, constr=FALSE, hyper=list(prec = list(initial = log(0.001), fixed=TRUE))) +
  ##  If the initial precision for epsilon is too low then model will fit terribly
  f(epsilon, constr = FALSE, hyper=list(prec = list(initial = log(0.1), fixed=TRUE)))

# Linear Combinations
fit <-  inla(formula, data = Y.inla, family = "poisson",
            control.predictor = list(compute=TRUE),
            control.compute=list(config=TRUE))
sam <- inla.posterior.sample(2000, fit)

My big question now is about the prior specification. Currently I pretty much have independent priors for every parameter in my model. In particular, I am a little worried about the ~ 600 (N x D) independent priors for epsilon terms when really there should only be ~ 50 (D x D)/2 in the form of the covariance matrix V. While it may not be so bad with only 60 samples, my real datasets have thousands and I worry this will get out of hand if it is scaling as N x D (plus its not really using the information in the data optimally).

Is there some way to rectify this situation and model the epsilons as sharing a covariance structure? I know there is a Wishart prior that goes up to 5 dimensions but it seems to stop there. Even if I modeled them as having diagonal covariance it would be better because at least then its sharing information across samples.

Hello Haakon,

Thank you very much for the tips of using the median, any strong reason that I should also change?

thanks

On Sunday, January 7, 2018 at 2:53:11 AM UTC-5, Haakon Bakka wrote:

> Hi,
>
> To interpret the pc prior, I usually compute the prior median for sigma (marginal standard deviation), which is the 1/lambda*log(2).
>
> # Your Models
> prior2 <- prior1 <-list(prec = list(prior = "pc.prec", param = c(1, .01)))
> l = 1*log(0.5)/log(0.1)
> giving 0.3
>
> prior3 <- prior1 <-list(prec = list(prior = "pc.prec", param = c(0.01, .01)))
> l = 0.01*log(0.5)/log(0.01)
> giving 0.0015
>
> prior4 <- prior1 <-list(prec = list(prior = "pc.prec", param = c(0.7, .01)))
> l = 0.7*log(0.5)/log(0.01)
> giving 0.1
>
> From this you can see that when the location parameter (prior median of sigma) is somewhere near the truth, you recover the truth. When it is very far away from the truth, you do not recover the truth.
>
> PS: Using the prior median to specify the prior, with param = c(prior.median, 0.5) is a choice I make personally. But I end up with the same prior distribution, usually, as people who prefer to specify the 0.01 quantile.
>
> Kind regards,
> Haakon
>
>
>

> On 3 January 2018 at 23:40, <gma...@ncsu.edu> wrote:

> >
> > We have experimented a set of penalized priors, however we notice something unusual precision see below in yellow.
> >
> > Basically for model “mod3” the mean precision for group is way higher than the posterior mean of random effects when we use "pc.prec", param = c(0.01, .01))? If we penalize up to .7 seems to be reasonable, is there any particular explanation?
> >
> > thank you very much
> >
> >

messages.subject: INLA on CRAN (new developments)
messages.subject_clean: INLA on CRAN (new developments)
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA devs,

Firstly, thanks for all your work on INLA. It is much appreciated.

I maintain a package (INLAutils) that adds ggplot2 support and other tweaks that I think useful to INLA. The package has been on CRAN for a year or so. However, my latest update to the package has been rejected for relying heavily on a package that is not on CRAN.

To quote the email.

"
Your package apparently heavbily relies on INLA, as you say in your submission comments and as the name of the package indicates.
How can you have a weak dependency on INLA then? Does your package make any sense without INLA?
If not, we believe you either have to convince the INLA maintainer to host INLA on a mainstream repository such as CRAN or you have to host your package elsewhere, e.g. somewhere alongside INLA?
"

I imagine this will subsequently affect other packages such as inlabru, excursions and INLABMA.

I am currently trying to persuade CRAN to accept my package anyway. But I also think I need to suggest (again) that anything you could do to get INLA on CRAN or even bioconducter would be very beneficial. As demonstrated by my package and the 3 packages mentioned above, and it's use by TMB, INLA is becoming the center of an ecosystem rather than a simple standalone package. Thinking long term about how best to distribute INLA and related packages would benefit everyone (and in that I acknowledge that your careers etc. may be your prime concern). If CRAN is not an option then perhaps you could think about hosting packages that depend on CRAN somewhere alongside it, as suggested in the email from CRAN. Or something. Or perhaps an actively maintained list of packages that use INLA is the easiest first step (which I will try to get around to doing myself).

I hope I don't come across as demanding of your time or effort. And thanks again for your work.

Tim

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

the CRAN maintainters have presented a moving target on this issue...

I believe that the building of the binaries on the different systems
is a solvable problem, though non-trivial (Solaris would be a
particular challenge due to the lack of testing environments and
different compilers).

In previous discussions one of the main stumbling blocks have been the
size and complexity; if they agree to having the documentation
examples disabled for running actual inla code that might be ok.

The other main issue has historically been the rapid update-cycle of
INLA, but for packages relying on INLA having less frequent updates on
CRAN could be beneficial

Haavard will have to weigh in as the person who actually deals with
the binary build; I don't think the fmesher part of the code will
present big problems that we haven't already solved for the excursions
package, but inla itself is a more complex beast.

TL&DR: I agree in principle, but I'm pretty sure we'll need help to
make this actually happen in a way that the CRAN maintainers can
accept.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

thanks for initiating this disucssion. This sounds like a 'change in
policy' or the interpretation of it, wrt to CRAN, about packages like
ours. Let me say that we have also faced similar issues/discussions
with papers submitted to Journal of Stat Software using INLA, but these
issues have been resolved so far.

>From my point of view:

- I have no objections to move INLA package into CRAN
- I do not want to spend all that hours/days/etc or work
  getting it there. if others want to give it a try...
- Yes, the fmesher build is relative straight forward, at least if the
X11 support is disabled.
- the inla-binary build is more a challenge, but still doable with
enough effort (and *maybe* some flexibility/help/adjustment from the
CRAN side)

- A package on CRAN with prebuildt binaries *is* a serious potential
security risk, and should not be allowed, and I agree on that of
course. I have never had problems that the R-INLA package is not on
CRAN [beyond the ``regular'' discussions with the JSS editors...]

A tempting workaround, is to use the same strategy, as R CORE MEMBER,
Martyn Plummer, use for JAGS.

- post the R interface package on CRAN
- require the jags binary to be build manually or downloaded from
somewhere else

I do not know why this is so for JAGS, as compiling JAGS is straight
forward.

We can in this case provide binaries to be downloaded, even semi-
automatic from within R, and add them to the package or installed
somewhere else. Otherwise, leave the user to compile it themself.

In any case, this would require to get the R-interface up2date when it
comes to documentation and pass all CRAN checks, but that is doable. if
this would again depend only on Finn & me, I would guess that
E[TimeToThatHappens] = infty.

All the best,

H

Yes, I essentially agree with all of that.

Just to clarify, when I mentioned having a separate package with the binaries, I meant that that package would work exactly the same does now, with prebuilt binaries not on CRAN. It would just be easier for users to install than installing prebuilt binaries some other way.  To be clear, my ideal preference is that no prebuilt binaries are distributed _at_all_, but that requires a more portable build system than we currently have.

I would be happy to share the testing system I use on Linux to do the CRAN checks; some of the current issues are straightforward to fix. Others less so.

Finn

> > Dear INLA devs,

Thanks Dr. Rue for your reply. Also thanks for the paper. I got the chance to read it earlier.

The main issue is, in my dataset, I have weight for each individual. Even your paper says that "The wij are known weights defined for each observed data points".

The inla function is written in a way that if we had one single weight (say, 0.4583) assigned to all individuals in the data, it will do this,

> rep(0.4583, dim(df)[1])

That way, all the individuals are receiving the same weight 0.4583. Since we have different weights for different individuals, so all the weights are being replicated. With my limited programming and statistical knowledge that's what I understood.

Is there any way that inla will use only the assigned weights to each individuals while carrying out the analysis?

Thanks in advance. Really appreciate your effort.

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I have used the INLA-SPDE to control the spatial effects in a regression on housing data.
However, several covariates are categorical variables.
When I try to interpret the results of the regression, I find that the results just show a coefficient of the corresponding categorical variable. On the contrary, some categorical variable (polytomous variable) owns more than two levels, how can I interpret these categorical variables using one coefficient?

I upload my R file and dataset file in the attachment

Best wishes
Charles

No one suggested that a package would download binaries. What I suggested was that just as now, there would be a non-CRAN package that would have the binary part of inla. This would be as an alternative to having users manually install it using other tools outside of R, which would be much harder for Mac and Windows users.
That R would be involved in the installation of that wouldn’t necessarily involve CRAN at all. R would just be ablation tool like any other installation tool for precompiled binaries.

But again, my preference is that we fix the build system...

Finn

messages.body_plain:
I've created a new mini-repository with my special builder/checker tool here:
  https://bitbucket.org/finnlindgren/simple-inla-builder
I've only used it on Linux, since that's the only system we have a
build.user Makefile,
but the principle should work on Mac as well.

While checking that this should work for others, I remembered that
another practical issue is
that most of the INLA package documentation is autogenerated from
comments, similarly
but not identically to how roxygen works.  Making an R package would
likely need to either
convert all of that into roxygen2 format, or integrate the current
format into a CRAN-compatible
method, or make the current method, where some autogenerated code is
actually stored in the
repository (beware of conflicts if two people run the
autogeneration!), safer to use.

PS. mercurial again, sorry Tim. ;-)

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] INLA with survey data: throwing error
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] INLA with survey data: throwing error
messages.body_plain:
The new testing-version of today Version_18.02.14, accept argument
'weights' with family='coxph'.

this argument, will simply assign weight w[i] to datapoint i. since in
coxph, datapoint i is expanded into a poisson counts yy[j], yy[j+1],
..., yy[j+k],  and all these poisson counts will inherit the weight of
the orgiginal datapoint, w[i].

If this is what you want, is something I cannot answer to...

Best
H

> statistical knowledge that's what I understood.

> Thanks in advance. Really appreciate your effort.
>
>

> > >

> y=xB+e A+ epsilon

> y:T*N

> B:K*N
> e: T*r
> A:r*N
> epsilon:T*N
> s.t: N:number of spatial points   T:time points   r: autoregressive coefficient (here consider r=1)

>

>

messages.subject: Re: Unexpected flat maps
messages.subject_clean: Unexpected flat maps
messages.body_plain:
I'm incurring in the same problem. Checking the convergence of the MCMC procedures on the prior parameter, I have performed comparable results between MCMC and INLA changing the prior distribution.
WINBUGS has the following default for the prior Gamma distribution
prior.iid = c(0.001,0.001)
prior.besag = c(0.1,0.1)
which are quite informative, especially the spatial one.

In the BYM example with R-INLA (http://www.r-inla.org/examples/volume-1/code-for-bym-example), the following priors were suggested
prior.iid = c(1,0.01)
prior.besag = c(1,0.001)
but they are less informative and the estimates may getting worse when you manage with rare diseases and then a low number of cases (see Carroll et al. 2015).

P.

Il giorno mercoledì 28 settembre 2016 14:23:22 UTC+2, Hèctor Perpiñán ha scritto:
>
> Hello INLA experts!
>
>
>
> We have been working with some disease mapping models in an extensive study in the Valencian Region (Spain) and have found some results that we find a bit puzzling. We have been fitting the BYM proposal for a lot of diseases and in occasions we have found some striking flat maps that we considered unreliable. For checking this, we have further fitted those same models in WinBUGS and we have found that the something weird was happening in those results. At least the maps from WinBUGS differed sometimes substantially from those in INLA.
>
>
> We are attaching a Markdown document (https://drive.google.com/open?id=0BwbigALl4QRYMVd3Y2hWeWNVNVk) with a clear example of what we are referring to. At the beginning of the document you will find the code used for fitting the models. We have fitted this for Asthma for different periods of time. You will see that for shorter periods INLA results are markedly different from those in WinBUGS. At the beginning they are flat and they progressively resemble those in WinBUGS when the number of periods is growing. WinBUGS results from the very beginning resemble the results obtained with longer periods. At the end of the document you will also find a graph with the posterior mean of the log-precisions (for both random effects in BYM) for both WinBUGS and INLA runs. They are markedly different, mainly for the heterogeneous random effects. For the shorter periods both log-precision estimates go to the same value and this value does not change for the heterogeneous effect although the data are different. Surprisingly, for other datasets (pancreatic cancer) we have found both posterior distributions to converge to exactly these same values. Moreover, we have changed the starting point in INLA for these values ( c(1,1), c(2,2) or c(10, 10)) and we have found that regardless this initial value, the trace of these posterior means converge to the values displayed at the markdown document. So the posterior mean does not get stuck at these values from the very starting point of the INLA iterative algorithm. On the contrary they do converge to the values pointed out.
>
>
> You will see at our document that we have used a uniform prior distribution on the positive real line for the standard deviations since this is the usual choice that we make. But we have also tried a Cauchy prior on the sd as also suggested in the literature and already implemented in INLA and we get the same results. We have also tried with the different approximations used in INLA, such as simplified Laplace, but nothing changes. As mentioned, we have also found this issue with other diseases like pancreatic cancer which present more cases than asthma:
>
> 2000 --> 414 cases
>
> 2000-2003 --> 1646 cases
>
> 2000-2006 --> 2971 cases
>
> 2000-2009 --> 4501 cases
>
> 2000-20012 --> 6356 cases
>
> 2000-2014 --> 7647 cases
>
>
>
> Do you have any idea about what could be happening here? Why INLA patterns don’t appear until the 2nd or 3rd maps and WinBUGS detect a pattern first? If uniform priors on the sd does not favour flat maps, why do INLA returns flat maps when little information is available (this is not what the prior would be saying)? Are we missing out something?
>
>
>
> Thanks for your help.
>
> Hèctor
>
>
>

messages.subject: How to fit models with multivariate outcome with INLA
messages.subject_clean: How to fit models with multivariate outcome with INLA
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am trying to fit a model with three outcomes. Since my data is multilevel and bayesian regression modeling gives more flexibility, I am trying to fit a multilevel model using INLA.

I have three outcomes. I was wondering if I could fit a single multivariate model. I went through help pages with examples of multiple likelihood and also referred to another paper that uses bivariate outcome and applied INLA: "A latent process model for forecasting multiple time series in environmental public health surveillance", Morrison et al 2016.

My code snippet for implement is as follows:

n <- nrow(data_in)
Y <- matrix(NA, n*3, 3)
Y[1:n, 1] <- data_in$Outcome1
Y[(1+n):(3*n), 1] <- NA # faked observations
Y[(1+n):(2*n), 2] <- data_in$Outcome2   # actual observations
Y[c(1:n,((2*n+1):(3*n)) ), 2] <- NA # faked observations
Y[(1+2*n):(3*n), 3] <- data_in$Outcome3   # actual observations
Y[c(1:(2*n) ), 3] <- NA # faked observations

x <- data_in[,c("P_ID", "var1","var2","var3")]
X <- rbind(x,x,x)

Y <- data.frame(Y)
names(Y) <- c("Outcome1","Outcome2","Outcome3")

formula_tv = list(Outcome1, Outcome2, Outcome3) ~ var1 + var2 + var3 +  f(P_ID, model="iid")
system.time(
result_tv <- inla(formula_tv, family = c("Gaussian","Gaussian","Gaussian"), data = cbind(Y,X), control.compute=list(dic=TRUE) )
)
summary(result_tv)

I guess the above model assumes that outcome is a trivariate normal distribution and returns single set of coefficients for the latent field.

I was wondering if there is a way to get three sets of coefficients, one for each outcome; similar to a multivariate regression model, that also accounts for covariance between outcomes.

Thank you,

Karthik S

In INLA, there is one formula for everything, which means that you have to hack together a formula, e.g.
~ var1.1 + var1.2 + var1.3
where you use many NA values to separate var1 into these three var's

To get covariance between outcomes, I suggest trying to share the iid model between the three familys, e.g. P_ID = rep(1:n, 3).

Does anyone have a simple code example for this?

Haakon

f(time,x, model="rw1", constr=FALSE)

will give you a RW1, Z(time), say, with 'weights' x(time), so the

this would be a generalization of \beta * x, where 'beta' is allowed to
vary over time.

messages.subject: Problem with changing posterior even when we set the prior SD to 0
messages.subject_clean: Problem with changing posterior even when we set the prior SD to 0
messages.body_plain:
Hi all! I was wondering if someone would be able to help me with a problem I am getting with INLA. Currently I am working with a spatio-temporal model, written with the following code. Just a couple notes about the model: the temporal component is defined by the "insptime" variable, and the second line of the code that defines datapred reflects that we only want predictions for the 4th insptime.

The problem is that in the code we use below, in the section that we have highlighted in red, we change the standard deviation of the prior of the model from prec = list(Intercept=0.1, not_sprayed=0.1)) to prec = list(Intercept=0.0, not_sprayed=0.0)), but when we look at the results of result$summary.fixed, the covariate and intercept of the model are still changing. We were wondering if anyone had any ideas about why they may be changing, even when we set the standard deviations of the priors to 0?

The code we used is below:

#===================================================================================
# IVb. Set up data in INLA format
#===================================================================================

# create datasets of observations
dataforfit <- df[which(df$outcome == 1 | df$outcome == 0),]
datapred <- df[which(df$insptime == 4),]

# print out number of observations of each timestep
print(paste0("Number of observations from time step 1: ", length(which(dataforfit$insptime == 1))))
print(paste0("Number of observations from time step 2: ", length(which(dataforfit$insptime == 2))))
print(paste0("Number of observations from time step 3: ", length(which(dataforfit$insptime == 3))))
print(paste0("Number of observations from time step 4: ", length(which(dataforfit$insptime == 4))))

# print out sizes of dataforfit and datapred
print(paste0("Size of dataforfit: ", nrow(dataforfit)))
print(paste0("Size of datapred: ", nrow(datapred)))

# define time dimension
k <- length(unique(df$insptime))

# define two coordinate matrices
coords1<- cbind(dataforfit$LONGITUDEscale, dataforfit$LATITUDEscale)
coords <- cbind(datapred$LONGITUDEscale, datapred$LATITUDEscale)

# create mesh
mesh1 <- inla.mesh.2d(coords1, max.edge=c(50*S,50*S), cutoff=0.2)

# create two A matrices
A.est <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh=mesh1,
                          loc=coords1,
                          group=dataforfit$insptime,n.group=k)

A.prd <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh=mesh1, loc=coords, group=datapred$insptime)

# create SPDE object of Matern covariance matrix
spde <- inla.spde2.matern(mesh1,
                          alpha=2,
                          theta.prior.mean=c(8,-5),
                          theta.prior.prec=c(0.1,0.1))

# create mesh index
mesh.index <- inla.spde.make.index(name='spatial',
                                   n.spde=spde$n.spde,n.group=k)

# create stack object for data for fit
stack.est =
  inla.stack(data=list(y=dataforfit$outcome),
             A=list(A.est,1),
             effects=
               list(c(mesh.index,list(Intercept=1)),
                    list(
                      not_sprayed=dataforfit$not_sprayed)),
             tag="est")

# create stack object for data for prediction
stack.pred =
  inla.stack(data=list(y=datapred$outcome),
             A=list(A.prd,1),
             effects=
               list(c(mesh.index,list(Intercept=1)),
                    list(
                      not_sprayed=datapred$not_sprayed)),
             tag="pred")

# combine stack objects
stack = inla.stack(stack.est, stack.pred)

# formula to input into INLA
formula <- y ~ -1 + Intercept + not_sprayed + f(spatial,
                                                model=spde,
                                                group=spatial.group,
                                                control.group=list(model='ar1',
                                                                   hyper=list(theta=list(prior='pccor1', param=c(0, 0.9)))))

#===================================================================================
# IVc. Run INLA model
#===================================================================================

# priors are set by control.fixed
result <- inla(formula,
               data = inla.stack.data(stack, spde=spde),
               family = c("binomial"),verbose=TRUE,
               #control.predictor = list(A=inla.stack.A(stack), compute=TRUE,link=1)  # Produces estimates
               control.predictor = list(A=inla.stack.A(stack), compute=TRUE,link=1, precision=.001)  # sets the precision on the A matrix low should speed things up!
               ,control.inla = list(reordering = "metis")
               ,control.fixed = list(mean = list(Intercept=-6.9, not_sprayed=1.17), # Prior means
                                     prec = list(Intercept=0.1, not_sprayed=0.1))  #Prior standard deviations
               #,num.threads=4  # uses 4 cores may be helpful
)

# runs a second inla model starting at the median of the first one
result <- inla.rerun(result)

result.f <- inla.spde2.result(result, "spatial", spde, do.transf=TRUE)

Hi Justin,
prec is not the standard deviation. It's the inverse of the variance (the precision). You need to make it large if you want the standard deviation to be almost zero.

Best wishes

Dan

messages.body_plain:
Also,
I'm pretty sure you don't want to mess with the control.predictor
"precision" parameters, since that is a numerical method tweaking
parameter, and not a proper model parameter.
(And setting that precision to a small value means that you decouple
your observations from the latent variables, so your estimates and
predictions will be meaningless...)

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am following the examples in Blangiardo, Cameletti et al. 2012, "Spatial and Spatio-Temporal models with R-INLA <http://www.math.ntnu.no/inla/r-inla.org/case-studies/Blangiardo-et-al-2012/Report-version-Oct-2012.pdf>”. I have a very simple question relating to the examples contained within that paper.

Following Eq 6 (p. 13) and the code for the “formula.1” model on p. 15, I wrote the model below for my data. There are eight years of data.

formula.1<- y ~ 1 + f(ID.area, model="bym", graph=adjGraph) + x1 + x2 + x3 + f(ID.area1, year, model="iid") + year

mod1 <- inla(formula.1, family=”poisson”, data=data, E=Exp, control.compute=list(dic=TRUE, cpo=TRUE), control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE))

## random effects associated with space-time interaction term ##

rfx.IDarea1 <- mod1$summary.random$ID.area1

Based on the explanation provided by Blangiardo/Cameletti, I understand that the above model has a linear trend (global time effect) and an area-specific trend (via the space-time interaction).

Here, the random effects for the space-time interaction only have one random effect for each area. The example Georgia births space-time interaction model has a non-linear time term - the inla.make.lincombs command is used - and there is one random effect for each area-year combination. Do I need to use inla.make.lincombs here, even though the time term is linear? And in “my” model, is there only one random effect per area for the space-time interaction because the main time trend in the model is linear?

I am just trying to understand these models, starting with the simplest. Thank you for your help!

Mercedes

messages.subject: Different probability results when running the model multiple times
messages.subject_clean: Different probability results when running the model multiple times
messages.body_plain:
Hi all, I was wondering if someone could provide some further clarification as to why our INLA model may be giving different results every time that we run our code.

I was reading about others having this similar problem here <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/r-inla-discussion-group/qkoV9ZtA1Wo>, but this question regarded different results on different computers. I am currently running the model multiple times on the same code. An example in difference of probabilities I am receiving is: 0.00430474561287514 vs. 0.0116855131964157

The code we used is below. Thanks in advance for any clarification!:

#===================================================================================
# IVb. Set up data in INLA format
#===================================================================================

# create datasets of observations
dataforfit <- df[which(df$outcome == 1 | df$outcome == 0),]
datapred <- df[which(df$insptime == 4),]

# print out number of observations of each timestep
print(paste0("Number of observations from time step 1: ", length(which(dataforfit$insptime == 1))))
print(paste0("Number of observations from time step 2: ", length(which(dataforfit$insptime == 2))))
print(paste0("Number of observations from time step 3: ", length(which(dataforfit$insptime == 3))))
print(paste0("Number of observations from time step 4: ", length(which(dataforfit$insptime == 4))))

# print out sizes of dataforfit and datapred
print(paste0("Size of dataforfit: ", nrow(dataforfit)))
print(paste0("Size of datapred: ", nrow(datapred)))

# define time dimension
k <- length(unique(df$insptime))

# define two coordinate matrices
coords1<- cbind(dataforfit$LONGITUDEscale, dataforfit$LATITUDEscale)
coords <- cbind(datapred$LONGITUDEscale, datapred$LATITUDEscale)

# create mesh
mesh1 <- inla.mesh.2d(coords1, max.edge=c(50*S,50*S), cutoff=0.2)

# create two A matrices
A.est <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh=mesh1,
                          loc=coords1,
                          group=dataforfit$insptime,n.group=k)

A.prd <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh=mesh1, loc=coords, group=datapred$insptime)

# create SPDE object of Matern covariance matrix
spde <- inla.spde2.matern(mesh1,
                          alpha=2,
                          theta.prior.mean=c(8,-5),
                          theta.prior.prec=c(0.1,0.1))

# create mesh index
mesh.index <- inla.spde.make.index(name='spatial',
                                   n.spde=spde$n.spde,n.group=k)

# create stack object for data for fit
stack.est =
  inla.stack(data=list(y=dataforfit$outcome),
             A=list(A.est,1),
             effects=
               list(c(mesh.index,list(Intercept=1)),
                    list(
                      not_sprayed=dataforfit$not_sprayed)),
             tag="est")

# create stack object for data for prediction
stack.pred =
  inla.stack(data=list(y=datapred$outcome),
             A=list(A.prd,1),
             effects=
               list(c(mesh.index,list(Intercept=1)),
                    list(
                      not_sprayed=datapred$not_sprayed)),
             tag="pred")

# combine stack objects
stack = inla.stack(stack.est, stack.pred)

# formula to input into INLA
formula <- y ~ -1 + Intercept + not_sprayed + f(spatial,
                                                model=spde,
                                                group=spatial.group,
                                                control.group=list(model='ar1',
                                                                   hyper=list(theta=list(prior='pccor1', param=c(0, 0.9)))))

#===================================================================================
# IVc. Run INLA model
#===================================================================================

# priors are set by control.fixed
result <- inla(formula,
               data = inla.stack.data(stack, spde=spde),
               family = c("binomial"),verbose=TRUE,
               #control.predictor = list(A=inla.stack.A(stack), compute=TRUE,link=1)  # Produces estimates
               control.predictor = list(A=inla.stack.A(stack), compute=TRUE,link=1)
               ,control.inla = list(reordering = "metis")
               ,control.fixed = list(mean = list(Intercept=-6.9, not_sprayed=1.17), # Prior means
                                     prec = list(Intercept=0.1, not_sprayed=0.1))  #Prior standard deviations
               #,num.threads=4  # uses 4 cores may be helpful
)

# runs a second inla model starting at the median of the first one
result <- inla.rerun(result)

result.f <- inla.spde2.result(result, "spatial", spde, do.transf=TRUE)

messages.body_plain:
You’re not running the model twice, you are running it more steps (rerun is similar to continuing the optimisation iterations) which makes a difference for models with illdefined logposterior maximum. With a binomial likelihood and and a very large prior standard deviations for the SPDE parameters it’s likely your posterior is problematic. (~3 is quite large when the field is used on the log-scale. How did you choose the spde prior settings? They look very strange! You should consider using the inla.spde2.pcmatern() model instead.)

What is the verbose output? I suspect your field parameter estimates diverge.

Finn

Hi Finn, thanks for the response (on this post and my other post)!

One thing is that I'm actually running this entire code twice, each time running the rerun function, but receiving different results. But what you said remains the same I think -- it could be our large prior standard deviations, that we actually should have changed to something like "theta.prior.prec=c(100,100))" and " prec = list(Intercept=0.1, not_sprayed=0.1))" later in the code.

We misunderstood that the precision was not the variance, but the inverse of the variance.

After reading more about inla.spde2.pcmatern(), I'm not sure I completely understand the difference between inla.spde2.pcmatern() and the inla.spde2.matern() function we are using -- the "pcmatern()" seems to be an update of the "matern()" but I am not completely sure about this. I can try it though!

I was also wondering what "verbose output" was? Are you referring to everything that is written in the console when the model is run?

Thanks so much for your help Finn!

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

multithreading can also lead to different results due to order of
operations (but usually not as large as the one you quoted; however,
if the model is ill-defined, I'd expect those differences to be more
noticeable than for well-defined models).

spde2.matern and spde2.pcmatern differ in the type of prior
distributions used for the parameters (see the help texts).  The spde
parameters used by the pcmatern version (range and std.dev <http://std.dev>.) is also
easier to interpret than the default spde2.matern parameterisation
(tau and kappa).
Have you read the "read this first" spde tutorial document on
r-inla.org <http://r-inla.org>? It gives a suggested way of setting the parameterisation
and priors for the regular spde2.matern model, which is similar in
spirit to what you can specify directly with the spde2.pcmatern model.

For verbose output, including a trace of the optimisation:
... <- inla(..., verbose=TRUE)

Finn

Finn

Your coordinate handling looks a bit odd. Exp(-5) as prior median for kappa means a very long range, but you seem to have some scaling of long/late involved as well.
I recommend drawing pictures of the data and the mesh to make sure it’s reasonable...

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] spatial and temporal model
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] spatial and temporal model
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

This is a space-time model, but we do not usually call it a space-time model.

When we say space-time we usually mean space-time interaction effect (very complicated and involving a mesh). What you write we refer to as a temporal model or a model with nonlinear covariates (there is no difference between a temporal effect and a non-linear effect).

An example with simulation-inference can be found here:
https://haakonbakka.bitbucket.io/btopic117.html

Kind regards,
Haakon Bakka

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Problem with INLA that I hope someone can help with
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Problem with INLA that I hope someone can help with
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I suggest you try with a simple simulation-inference example whenever you encounter a problem.

In this case, note that you are setting the prec (short for precision), not the standard deviation. The connection is sigma = prec^ (-1/2).

So setting prec to 0.0 sets the standard deviation to infinity.

Kind regards,
Haakon Bakka

I have a model (covariates + SPDE) that I need to use to predict over a grid with more than 27K points. The model takes about 15 minutes to run using the observed data alone and INLA crashes when I try to use the full grid for prediction. I am considering splitting the grid into smaller blocks and then fit each model separately, but I am not sure whether this will make all the predictions to be based on EXACTLY the same fitted model. I suspect that if I fit the same model with the same data and a different block for prediction then INLA can fit slightly different models. Is this correct? Then, what will be the best way to do this prediction in parallel?

Many thanks,

Virgilio

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Prediction over large grids with INLA
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Prediction over large grids with INLA
messages.body_plain:
My recommendation for large scale prediction is to either
1) predict onto the mesh points only, and interpolate the means and standard deviations to the grid afterwards, or
2) use posterior samples to evaluate on the grid

Method 2) is available in the predict() function if you use inlabru. With raw inla, you’ll have to deal with inla.stack for the inla call and inla.posterior.sample for the samples.

Method 1) in raw inla still requires inla.stack, but the postprocessing is a simple inla.mesh.project call.

Finn
